DAMP methods, definitions, and analysis map

This appendix preserves the definitions, controls, calculation details, and notebook-to-report map behind the final report. Scientific interpretations are developed in the seven section reports and preliminary analyses; implementation results are collected in reproducibility. Figures discussed here are displayed alongside the methods that use them.

The appendix gives formulas as well as the reading-level explanations in the companions. A source is one of the eight sequence collections; a cohort is the set of sequences eligible for a particular comparison. A residue is one amino acid in a peptide. K/R means lysine/arginine and D/E means aspartic acid/glutamic acid; C means cysteine. A component or related-sequence group joins observed terminal extensions and one-residue substitutions, directly or through intermediate sequences; it is not a verified evolutionary family. Strata are categories such as source plus exact sequence length. These definitions matter whenever a comparison changes its population or weighting.

Metric guide

A metric needs its quantity, unit, comparison set, and denominator. Unless a laboratory measurement is explicitly paired with a prediction, the metrics below describe model outputs or selection decisions rather than biological accuracy.

Metric What it measures and how to read it
Predicted MIC A concentration for the model's intended target; µM means micromoles per litre. Lower means the model predicts less peptide is needed. Different strain/condition targets and synthetic inactive labels can give the same unit different training meanings.
Pass fraction Count with prediction ≤ the stated cutoff, divided by the shared eligible sequence count. It is not the measured fraction of active peptides.
Shared shortlist fraction For two equal lists of size k: shared peptides / k. An inclusive pairwise count includes triple-shared entries. An exclusive UpSet bar counts only the exact marked membership. Intersection-over-union instead divides by the union and is a different metric.
Overall / selected-pool disagreement Overall disagreement counts exactly-one-pass cases / all paired eligible sequences. Selected-pool disagreement uses the same numerator / sequences passing either tool. Overall agreement instead counts joint passes plus joint rejections. Different denominators explain why apparently conflicting percentages can both be correct.
Classifier vote / retention fraction A positive vote meets the stated score rule, not a common calibrated probability. Mixed means at least one positive and one negative. Retention is the number surviving a filter / the original model-specific shortlist size.
Fold spread / log2 range For positive predictions, fold spread = largest/smallest and log2 range = log2(fold spread). Ratios 1, 2, and 4 correspond to log2 ranges 0, 1, and 2. A twofold sequence-pair response counts pairs with ratio ≥2; it is not the direction of the edit or a correctness score.
Signed log2 ratio / offset log2(right/left) is +1 when right is twice left and −1 when half. An offset summarizes numerical displacement on that scale. Centering subtracts a model's median log prediction; it is a diagnostic transformation rather than calibration to measurements.
Percentile / rank gap Percentile is 100 × average tied rank / eligible count; lower is more favored for MIC. Rank gap is the maximum minus minimum percentile for one peptide across models. Percentage-point changes in this gap describe placement, not MIC changes or probabilities of error.
Spearman / Kendall / Pearson correlation Spearman summarizes agreement in ranks, Kendall in pair ordering with ties handled, and Pearson linear co-variation of its stated inputs. Values range from −1 to +1. High correlation can coexist with scale offsets or changing shortlists and is not a percentage of accurate predictions.
Cohen's kappa (observed agreement − expected agreement)/(1 − expected agreement), where expected agreement uses each classifier's marginal positive fraction. Zero matches that independence reference; one means identical labels. It is not accuracy and depends on class prevalence.
MAE / RMSE / signed difference MAE averages absolute differences; RMSE takes the square root of the mean squared difference, weighting large gaps more. A signed difference retains direction, as defined in the table. Units match the compared values, including log units when used. Prediction–prediction differences are disagreement; prediction–measurement differences are sample-specific errors with that sample's validation limits.
SD / CV / median absolute deviation SD measures spread around a mean; sample SD uses n−1 in the variance denominator. CV divides SD by the absolute mean. Median absolute deviation here is the unscaled median distance from the median. Across mixed targets, these are numerical summaries rather than assay repeatability or uncertainty.
Composition entropy / charge proxy Entropy is −sum(p_a log2 p_a) in bits, where p_a is a residue fraction; it describes diversity, not fold. Charge proxy is (K+R−D−E)/length, not full pH-dependent charge. Fractions can be reported per peptide or pooled over residues; the weighting must be stated.
PCA / decomposition variance fraction PC1's fraction is the share of variation in the stated numerical matrix captured by one fitted axis. Other variance fractions depend on their named decomposition and target panel. They are not predictive R², accuracy, or evidence of a biological mechanism. A covariance fraction is not a variance fraction.
Implementation-check count The number of successful numerical/software assertions. Repetition across thresholds is useful verification, not independent scientific replication.

A change from 10% to 20% is 10 percentage points, not a 10% relative change. Tables and plots use their stated shared populations; missing predictions are excluded rather than counted as failures. The model review explains which output differences limit biological interpretation.

What was reproduced

Calculation reproduction and sampled inference replay are documented in reproducibility. They establish implementation consistency, not biological accuracy.

Corrections and qualifications

Issue Assessment and action
DeepAMP replay tolerance Actual maximum absolute difference is 6.1713788959 × 10⁻⁶ log2 units. The original strict bound of 6 × 10⁻⁶ was slightly too small. Report and notebook prose now use 6.2 × 10⁻⁶. Scientific interpretation is unchanged.
“Low disagreement” Valid for the stated raw log2-range definition; cannot stand in for confidence, reliability, rank agreement, or experimental robustness. New per-model percentiles make this concrete.
Length and entropy The raw-tail contrast reproduces. Length reverses under centered/rank definitions. Entropy is constrained by sequence length and is not structural complexity. New source/exact-length residuals substantially attenuate its contrast.
Matching on predicted potency A conditional descriptive comparison of model outputs. It can introduce selection effects and cannot estimate a causal sequence effect. Direct high/low matching has poor common support.
Near-random shortlists Unconditional random overlap is a useful reference, but not a sufficient conclusion. Conditional source/length references show excess agreement despite small absolute overlap. No p values are inferred from these references.
Family weighting Terminal components capture one relationship, not all homology. New one-representative analysis strengthens this particular sensitivity without creating independent biological replicates.
Experimental validation Original 13 numeric labels remain exposure-limited. Additional archaeasin source data exist, but inferred identifiers, chemistry differences, selection, and censoring prevent a general model-ranking claim.
Assay variability Different strain/condition targets can disagree systematically. Neither literature-wide variation nor within-species label contrasts estimate a universal noise allowance for these predictions.

Original CSVs and executed outputs are preserved. Only the small replay-bound wording and pointers to the reviewed interpretation were changed in the earlier reports/notebook. Obsolete one-time construction scripts were removed; retained numerical scripts remain the reproducible sources.

New question 1: what does agreement mean to a screening decision?

The question here is whether agreement in concentration also means agreement on which peptides to choose. Log2 expresses predictions in doubling steps. A low or high tail is the lowest or highest 5% under the stated disagreement score; the middle comparison uses the remaining sequences between the two tails. Percentiles in this section are fractions from 0 to 1, so a gap of 0.50 means 50 percentage points; later tables sometimes express them directly on a 0–100 scale.

Let z(i,m) = log2(predicted MIC) for sequence i and model m. Raw disagreement is max_m z(i,m) − min_m z(i,m). Centering subtracts each model's cohort median; rank disagreement instead uses max-minus-min within-model percentile. Centered values are dimensionless relative predictions, not concentrations.

In the raw low tail, median model percentiles are 0.0958, 0.7161, and 0.7849 for APEX 1.1, MBC-Attention, and AMPredictor. The median within-sequence percentile range is 0.5708. Raw high and middle groups have corresponding ranges 0.5871 and 0.3020. This is the most useful new interpretation: similar absolute predictions can mark very different positions in each model's own distribution.

The high/low length contrast also changes:

Definition Low-tail median length High-tail median length
Raw log2 range 14 36
Model-median-centered log2 range 26 17
Within-model percentile range 24 20

Quantile cutoffs include ties; the percentile low tail contains 9,749 sequences, whereas the other tails contain 9,748. These are newly defined tails, not the original groups after simply changing their labels.

Evidence: group interpretation, transition table, definition-dependent profiles, Figure 2.

The figure below connects these definitions to the original selected groups: similar exported concentrations can still occupy different positions in each model's distribution.

New question 2: does small overlap mean absence of shared signal?

An expected intersection is the average number of shared selections under a specified hypothetical selection rule. It is useful as a reference for shared preferences, not as an estimate of correct selections.

For shortlists of size k from N sequences, independent uniform random lists have expected intersection k²/N. More relevant references can preserve each model's selected count within strata. With stratum size N(g) and selected counts A(g) and B(g), expected intersection is the sum over g of A(g)B(g)/N(g). The formula requires conditional uniformity and independence; it is a descriptive selection reference rather than a biological null model.

For the top 1% lists on all complete cases:

Pair Observed shared Unconditional reference Source + exact-length reference
APEX 1.1 / MBC 42 19.51 15.09
APEX 1.1 / AMPredictor 33 19.51 12.81
MBC / AMPredictor 107 19.51 44.33

There is shared signal relative to these references. There is still little agreement about which individual candidates occupy a small screening budget. These statements are compatible. Correlation and shortlist overlap answer different questions; neither evaluates accuracy without observations.

The new terminal-component sensitivity first constructs components across the full input by exact one-residue terminal trimming, with shorter length at least eight. In each component with complete predictions, it selects the sequence with the lexicographically smallest SHA256 hash. No prediction is used for this selection. There are 124,085 representatives, with 732 components spanning more than one source label. Each representative retains its own source label. Components and representative selection change the population and do not fully remove homology. Restricting to this population preserves small overlaps.

Evidence: all shortlist estimates and references, Figure 3.

The figure below compares shortlist overlap and rank behavior across source collections and the stated population restrictions. It shows whether a pooled summary survives those changes in what is counted.

New question 3: which disagreement survives scale alignment?

Pairwise median-offset removal subtracts the median of z(left) − z(right). It is slightly different from subtracting each model's separate median. Both are prediction-only diagnostics; neither fits an experimental calibration.

For the APEX versions on the common 194,947-sequence universe, pairwise twofold agreement rises from 16.65% to 80.22% after offset removal. The same operation raises APEX 1.1 / AMPredictor from 2.40% to 40.92%. All shortlist identities remain unchanged because the transformations preserve order. These diagnostics isolate an offset sensitivity, not the fraction of prediction error due to offsets.

An opposite-order pair has one model preferring the first peptide (lower MIC) and another preferring the second. Only pairs strictly ordered by both models enter that fraction; equal predictions are ties. The next formula handles those ties explicitly.

Opposite-order fractions are computed from exact Kendall tau-b together with each model's tie counts and joint ties. If P is the total number of sequence pairs, T(left/right) are model-specific tied pairs, and T(both) are jointly tied pairs, the strictly comparable count is Q = P − T(left) − T(right) + T(both). The concordant-minus-discordant count is tau-b times the square root of (P − T(left))(P − T(right)). The discordant fraction is then (Q minus that count)/(2Q). This avoids misreading (1 − tau-b)/2 when ties occur. Results are deterministic finite-collection summaries, not iid hypothesis tests.

Leave-one-source-out centering estimates model offsets on the other seven collections before applying them to the held-out source. It reduces median spread in every source, but Archaeomics retains 5.39-fold versus 3.78-fold under local centering. This shows some source dependence of offsets without using any truth labels. It is not held-out predictive calibration.

An exact log-scale covariance decomposition separates covariance of source means from mean within-source covariance. Between-source means contribute 39.5% and 38.6% of pooled log covariance for APEX 1.1 versus MBC and AMPredictor, respectively. These are fractions of covariance, not explained prediction variance, rank correlation, or causal source effects.

Evidence: scale and ranking, source offset transfer, covariance decomposition.

New question 4: what survives a local sequence contrast?

Entropy residualization subtracts the mean composition entropy among sequences from the same source and exact length, then compares the remaining deviations. It asks whether a diversity difference remains after those background differences are reduced.

Source/exact-length entropy residualization reduces the raw high-minus-low entropy difference from 0.732 to 0.094 bits. This is a population-standardized descriptive contrast, not a matched causal estimate. There is no justification for assuming residues in each peptide are independent draws from a stationary distribution to manufacture an entropy correction.

Among 92,225 observed terminal-extension pairs with complete predictions, APEX 1.1 and AMPredictor both change at least twofold for 400 pairs, of which 147 change in opposite directions. That is 36.8% of those selected strong-change pairs but only 0.159% of all eligible extension pairs. Reporting the selected denominator alone would exaggerate prevalence. Pairs share sequences and components; no independence or measured activity cliff is inferred.

An inactive-label proximity check was also deliberately tested. APEX 1.1 predictions ≥500 µM occur in 6.65% of the raw high tail versus 9.11% of the middle group. Thus, a simple “extreme disagreement is concentrated at an APEX 512 µM ceiling” story is unsupported by this diagnostic. Some predictions exceed 512; this is not a hard output ceiling. Label handling remains a possible source of distributional differences, not an established cause.

Evidence: entropy sensitivity, terminal-pair results, individual opposed-change examples, inactive-label proximity.

Additional experimental source recovered: useful but provisional

The earlier analysis correctly rejected supplementary files 3 and 4 as composition p values rather than measurements. However, the paper's Source Data Fig. 2 workbook contains the 80-peptide measured-activity table. Its Extended Data Fig. 4 workbook contains prediction/label pairs. The paper selected the cohort using APEX 1.1 predictions, and documents coding inactive labels as 512 µM; it is therefore a selected, label-processed cohort. Publication and methods

The exact supplementary downloads and synthesis-certificate archive are retained with URLs, retrieval date, and SHA256 hashes in archaeasin_curation_manifest.json. The archive hash matches the public Mendeley file metadata. Mendeley dataset v3

Identity linkage is inferred, not an explicit published identifier join. The measurement rows are numbered Archaeasin-1–80 but do not contain sequences. For each row, the new script matches the 11-target published prediction vector to the same 11 TSV outputs. Every best match has maximum absolute log2 difference <0.01; every runner-up is >0.05. Dropping each target in turn preserves every match, and the 80 predicted sequence matches are unique. Measured labels are never used in matching. This is strong provenance evidence but remains a numerical reconstruction requiring author confirmation of numbered identities.

The chemical audit catches a real discrepancy. Seventy-nine reconstructed base sequences exactly match the 80 synthesis certificates. Archaeasin-31 maps to predicted sequence KWKKLIKGFVINKF, whereas the otherwise unmatched certificate specifies VKWKKLIKGFVINKF. The extra N-terminal valine makes it a different chemical entity. That row is excluded; its E. coli measurement is 32 µM. The certificate comparison confirms base sequence and TFA salt, while terminal modifications remain independently unresolved. No silent terminal trimming is used.

The label audit catches a second issue. E. coli has 38 numeric source-data measurements and 42 blanks. All numeric cells match the corresponding extended-data labels exactly after log2 conversion; all blanks are coded there as log2 MIC = 9, or 512 µM. That code must not become an exact observed concentration. After the chemistry exclusion, 37 numeric measurements and 42 source-coded inactive rows remain. Their exact cached APEXDB and AMPredictor-training overlaps are both zero. This limited audit does not exclude all training exposure or homology for every model/checkpoint.

The numeric-only diagnostics are deliberately supplemental:

Model Numeric n Mean absolute log2 error Spearman correlation
APEX 1.0 37 1.121 −0.003
APEX 1.1 37 1.271 0.016
MBC-Attention 37 1.562 0.322
AMPredictor 37 1.911 0.387

These calculations condition on a measurable, selected potency range and omit the 42 source-coded inactive rows. They do not rank generalization. The apparent ordering depends on the objective: the smallest numeric error and strongest numeric rank correlation occur in different models. Endpoint mismatch, source selection, limited dynamic range, sample size, uncertain numbered identifiers, and unresolved chemistry still matter. They also show why the exceptionally small APEX 1.1 error in the original 13 exposed labels should not be generalized.

The output table includes a separate conditional diagnostic interpreting source inactives as >64 µM, the documented upper test concentration. Under that assumption, 90.5–97.6% of those rows receive ≤64 µM predictions across the four outputs. This is a sensitivity to the inactive interpretation, not a primary accuracy estimate. Neither the script nor this report imputes 512 as their true MIC.

Before promoting this cohort into a benchmark, confirm the numbered sequence map, resolve Archaeasin-31 and terminal chemistry, preserve censoring bounds, audit all training corpora, and state that evaluation is conditional on APEX selection. It can answer a selected-cohort question; it cannot supply a neutral estimate of discovery performance across all DAMP sources.

Evidence: curation script, provisional sequence map, certificate sequences, curated provisional E. coli records, numeric and conditional diagnostics, publication coding sensitivity.

Further falsification audit: methods and limits

stress_test_findings.py reads the original TSV and prior curation outputs without changing them. It writes all additional results under outputs/sanity_checks. Its execution manifest records the input checksum, runtime, software versions, seeds, and 32 passing computational checks. These checks are validations of arithmetic, provenance, and invariants; their count is not a measure of biological confidence. The checks were designed after inspecting earlier results and remain exploratory.

The main report now contains the numerical tables and reportable interpretations. The following details explain what each stress test can and cannot establish.

Independent calculation and perturbation checks

Shortlists are compared between NumPy partition selection and pandas selection, and before/after row permutation. All four models have a single sequence at the 1% cutoff; no arbitrary boundary tie can account for their tiny intersections. The pair-reversal formula is verified against explicit enumeration of all pairs in a 250-sequence sample rounded to introduce ties. Invariance to a common concentration-unit change and log-base change is also checked.

For bounded perturbations, each log2 score receives independent uniform noise in [−b,b], for b = 0.01, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, and 1. Each bound has 25 repeats. Original-versus-perturbed same-model overlap and perturbed-versus-perturbed cross-model overlap are both reported. The noise is deliberately hypothetical; no claim is made that model stochasticity, assay variation, or retraining error is independent, uniform, or of this size. The min/median/max summaries describe the specified simulation and are not confidence intervals.

Evidence: boundary/tie counts, perturbation summaries, individual runs.

Pair margins and budget dependence

Uniform index pairs are sampled with replacement using a fixed seed, and identical indices are excluded, leaving 1,999,991 sampled pairs. The sample is not a set of independent biological observations; it approximates a statistic of a fixed prediction matrix. Reversals are reported conditional on both models showing absolute log2 differences greater than 0, 0.5, 1, or 2. Each conditional fraction is accompanied by its eligible-pair count and fraction.

This changes the interpretation of APEX version disagreement: its approximately 19.7% all-pair reversal fraction falls to 1.47% for differences greater than twofold in both models. The corresponding cross-family fractions remain approximately 20–25%. A model-version shortlist can change substantially while its large pairwise potency distinctions are broadly preserved.

Absolute budgets of 100–20,000 candidates and directed cross-model percentile positions document where list differences occur. In particular, the directed margin test compares each model to its own cutoff, so arbitrary log intercepts cannot create or remove that criterion.

Evidence: margin-dependent reversals, budget dependence, directed shortlist positions.

Source restriction and missing-score bounds

The new population analyses remove each source, the two APEX-selected collections together, the database collection, or exact matches to the two cached training corpora. Within-source 1% budgets are also combined, yielding 1,953 candidates per model. None of these operations establishes an unbiased discovery population or complete exclusion of training exposure.

The missing-score bound uses fixed k = 1,950. Starting from a pairwise-complete universe, a model can lose old shortlist members only to newly admitted candidates. A conservative maximum number of replacements is its own missing-score count plus the count of newly admitted known scores no higher than its old cutoff, capped at k. If these replacement bounds are r(left) and r(right) and the old intersection is I, then a conservative new-intersection bound is:

max(0, I − r(left) − r(right)) ≤ new intersection ≤ min(k, I + min(r(left),r(right))).

Old candidates cannot newly enter a model's list when only extra candidates are added. Any gained intersection must therefore involve an added row. The bound is checked against 50 arbitrary log-score completions for each pair. These completions test implementation, not whether every possible completion has been enumerated or whether the loose bound is attainable. The derivation supplies the guarantee. Extrapolation into MBC's excluded short-length domain remains hypothetical.

Evidence: population sensitivities, source-proportional budgets, missingness bounds and random completion checks.

Broader sequence dependence

A graph represents sequences as points and observed edit relationships as links, or edges. A connected component contains sequences reachable through any chain of those links. This lets the analysis reduce the influence of densely sampled variants without claiming to identify every biological family.

The graph adds equal-length one-substitution edges to exact terminal-extension edges. The substitution search is exact: within each length and deletion position, sequences sharing the remaining string differ only at that position. Processing one length/position at a time avoids an all-pairs search and retains the full dataset as possible connecting intermediates. Minimum length is eight for substitution edges and for the shorter member of terminal edges.

There are 111,162 full-input components and 110,491 with complete predictions. Single linkage can connect distant endpoints and should not be described as a homology threshold. The largest represented component has 2,073 sequences, so it is particularly important not to treat every component member as a replicate.

Twelve representative choices minimize SHA256(seed + sequence) within each component. They do not use predictions or experimental labels. Component-median prediction summaries provide another sensitivity, and component-set overlaps compare the original shortlists without requiring the same exact variant. All three approaches preserve small cross-family overlap. These results do not exclude more distant homologues, different-length internal indels, or dependence between disconnected components.

Evidence: component summary, membership map, representative sensitivity, original component-set overlap, component-median selection.

Permutation controls and reference dependence

A permutation control reassigns existing predictions to different sequence labels. This keeps the set of predicted values unchanged while breaking some correspondence to individual peptides, asking which patterns can arise from distributions and selection rules alone.

Independent model-wise permutations are run 30 times globally and 30 times within source/exact-length strata. Predictions and their corresponding global percentiles are permuted together, preserving each model's marginal distribution. The stratified variant also preserves its observed association with those strata, while destroying peptide-specific alignment within them. No p value is calculated; these are constructed controls for the interpretation of an exploratory score. They do not preserve all family structure or constitute a uniquely correct null model of peptide biology.

The observed raw-low-group rank spread is lower than either permutation reference. Thus, the finding that this group has large rank spread does not establish an unexpected class of biological failures. Similarly, source/length-preserving permutations retain a 20-residue high-minus-low length contrast, close to 22 observed. That is not an estimate that a certain percentage of a causal effect is explained by these factors.

Within-source and source/length percentiles are computed separately from the global percentiles. The equal-source-weighted ECDF gives every source the same total weight, with exact ties sharing their weighted midpoint. Small strata have coarse ranks. All these sensitivities retain large numerical-versus-priority differences, with different exact magnitudes.

Evidence: permutation runs, flat summary, rank-reference sensitivity, permutation figure.

The figure below puts the observed low-tail rank gap beside the independently reassigned controls. The distributions show constructed reference runs, rather than measurement uncertainty.

APEX label semantics: a concrete new qualification

A pseudo-label assigns an artificial numeric concentration to an observation without an exact measured MIC, for example one exceeding the assay's tested maximum. The version ratio below is the newer prediction divided by the older prediction for the same peptide. A single multiplier would make this ratio constant across prediction bands.

The original APEX methods assign observations above 128 µM an inactive pseudo-label of 140 µM; APEX 1.1 instead uses 512 µM for observations above the tested maximum. The resulting ratio is 3.657. This closely matches the observed median E. coli version ratio, 3.628, and aligns the eight matched-target median ratios to a range of 0.833–1.055. This is a plausible contributor to global scale differences, while changed data and fitted models prevent causal attribution. Original APEX methods, APEX 1.1 methods

The fixed factor is taken from published methods, not fitted to minimize an error on this cohort. It remains a diagnostic. The version ratio is not constant across prediction regimes, and none of the transformations demonstrates calibration against measured MIC. Same-strain and same-unit outputs therefore still need a label-processing audit before interpreting a scale change biologically. Stratifying a ratio by its own denominator can also induce apparent structure; the prediction-band analysis is a conditional sensitivity, not independent evidence of a causal dependence on potency.

Evidence: target-level scaling sensitivity, prediction-regime sensitivity, primary-source record, figure.

The figure below compares the newer/older APEX prediction ratio with the published pseudo-label multiplier across the older version's prediction bands. A changing ratio argues against a universal correction.

Experimental labels and loss functions

For numeric MIC M, the sensitivity interval is (M/2, M] under a monotone doubling-dilution threshold model. Every numeric E. coli value in this cohort is at least 4 µM, so the presumed lower dilution is within the published assay range. Distance in log2 space is zero inside the interval and the distance to the closest boundary outside it. For source-coded inactive rows, one-sided distance to (64, infinity) is used conditionally, without imputing an exact MIC. The open-boundary distance is its infimum; zero loss at the boundary is not an assertion of compatibility with a strict inequality.

These distances are compatibility losses and lower bounds on latent-threshold error, not actual MAE or estimated uncertainty. They do not model replicate variation or establish interval coverage. The different APEX ordering under numeric-only and all-row conditional losses demonstrates the importance of endpoint/censoring assumptions. A one-numeric-peptide deletion analysis shows that no single numeric outlier reverses the numeric-only ordering; it cannot repair systematic cohort selection or uncertain numbered identities.

All downloaded source hashes are rechecked, as are uniqueness and the recorded leave-target-out linkage checks. The number-to-sequence map remains inferred; rechecking a recorded fingerprint result is not equivalent to obtaining an author-confirmed identifier mapping.

Evidence: label/loss sensitivities, one-peptide deletions, new check results.

Claims to retain, demote, and exclude

Retain as main results: fixed-budget prioritization instability; same-strain version-dependent screening changes; scale/rank separation; definition-sensitive sequence associations; matched-target-panel correction; sampled preprocessing reproducibility.

Retain as supporting or exploratory analyses: source dependence, partial redundancy controls, conditional shortlist references, local sequence contrasts, training-domain hypotheses, and the provisional archaeasin diagnostic. Present raw-low-tail rank spread primarily as an agreement-definition warning; the new permutations limit its interpretation as an unexpected sequence-specific finding. Present APEX scale drift alongside the documented pseudo-label change.

Exclude as conclusions: best predictor; consensus as validated confidence; biological potency or source superiority from predicted MICs; cysteine, folding, or charge as the established mechanism; a universal experimental tolerance; a causal fraction of disagreement attributed to assay heterogeneity.

This is enough for a substantive computational final report. A publication-level superiority or discovery claim needs independent outcome evidence and a separate novelty assessment. The analysis should not be expanded indefinitely merely to increase the number of outputs.

Additional-trend extension

Additional-trend methods adds four exploratory questions beyond the disagreement tails. All original inputs and earlier output tables are retained. The script explore_additional_trends.py writes to outputs/additional_trends; its manifest records input and dependency hashes, denominators, and 25 passing checks. These checks confirm implementation and algebraic invariants, not biological accuracy.

Exact-composition comparisons

Sorting a sequence's residues produces an exact amino-acid-count signature. Grouping by that signature and source holds all analyzed composition descriptors fixed. There are 6,886 multi-member groups with 16,815 sequences. The primary comparison uses 5,410 exactly two-member groups so that differing group sizes cannot themselves generate different maximum-minus-minimum ranges. Both members have complete predictions for the same four E. coli outputs. Larger groups, source strata, and a cysteine-free length-8–39 restriction are reported separately.

The twofold-change fraction is 6.10% for APEX 1.1, 19.28% for MBC-Attention, and 15.53% for AMPredictor. Median fold differences are much smaller. Within-model percentile spreads are also reported because the models have different overall output dispersions. These are sensitivities to ordered sequence inputs, not a controlled comparison of architectures, proof that a model learned a biological motif, or an activity-cliff benchmark.

Two-member pairs have a fixed lexical orientation shared by every model; direction-agreement tables require each model to exceed the stated change margin. The terminal-position subset holds the observed core and added residue fixed while changing the terminus. Unordered longer-sequence pairs are deduplicated; the N/C longer sequences must have the same source, while the observed core's source need not be identical. These pairs overlap the composition analysis and are not independent corroboration. Terminal chemistry is not inferred from the sequence strings.

Evidence: composition summaries, source strata, domain sensitivity, shared pair list, direction agreement, terminal-position summary.

Classifier filtering as a pipeline choice

All four classifier outputs are available on the 194,947-sequence common MIC cohort. A positive decision means output ≥ the stated exploratory threshold; the binary AMP-CLIP output is unchanged at thresholds 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7. A classifier threshold is not assumed calibrated, and four votes are not four independent biological measurements.

At 0.5, unanimous filtering retains 76.97% of APEX 1.1's original 1,950-member list, 29.23% of MBC's, and 22.41% of AMPredictor's. The original list is selected before filtering, so the result measures attrition rather than a re-ranked list of unchanged size. Source/length reference rates are averaged over the actual selected candidates. Their excess-retention contrasts are descriptive and do not remove all composition, selection, or training-exposure effects.

The restriction and one-component-representative sensitivities recompute each model's lowest-MIC 1% list on their own population. The representative is selected without predictions by the minimum sequence SHA256 per observed component. General AMP labels and relative E. coli MIC ranks target different questions; neither the attrition numbers nor the unanimous-positive peptides outside the MIC top 10% estimate a false-positive rate.

Evidence: retention tables, vote-count and MIC-rank summaries, composition/filtering figure.

The figure below connects two separate screening questions: response to fixed-composition rearrangements on the left, and retention of MIC-shortlisted candidates by the classifier filter on the right. Each uses its own eligible set.

Relative target contrast

The target contrast compares typical predicted MICs for the four selected Gram-positive versus four selected Gram-negative targets. A geometric mean averages log concentrations and converts back; its ratio describes this particular panel, not universal selectivity. PC1 is the fitted direction capturing the most numerical variation, and a residual is what remains after removing the stated fitted relationship.

The Gram-group contrast uses the same eight unambiguous targets in both APEX versions. It is a difference of mean log2 predictions, equivalently a log2 ratio of geometric means. It removes a common log intercept and an arbitrary per-peptide additive term shared by every target. These invariances are checked directly. They do not remove a general-potency axis with unequal target-specific loadings.

The cross-version Spearman correlation is 0.734 on 195,625 sequences, positive in all eight sources, and 0.700 at component medians on the common 194,947-row cohort. Leave-one-target-out contrasts have three versus four targets or four versus three, with each remaining group re-averaged; correlations range 0.540–0.863. This panel sensitivity limits a claim of general Gram-class selectivity.

A further adjustment fits a cubic relationship between ranked contrast and ranked first principal component within each version. PCA uses deterministic full SVD on the eight-target log prediction matrix. The cross-version Pearson correlation of the rank residuals is 0.530; it is not another Spearman coefficient. The adjustment is fitted on the same finite collection and has no experimental calibration interpretation. It shows a remaining partial association under that particular general-potency control. The two model versions share development history, so their agreement is not independent biological validation.

Evidence: Gram contrast, all target-pair contrasts, leave-target-out sensitivity, component medians, potency-axis sensitivity.

Venomics and the analysis unit

This comparison asks whether the association describes all observed variants equally or gives each related group equal influence. Those are different sampling questions: a group supplying many similar peptides has more influence under equal sequence weights.

In the complete-case graph, Venomics has 4,618 rows, 401 represented components, and 57.2% of rows in its ten largest components. The charge proxy is (K + R − D − E) / length; it does not estimate pH-specific molecular charge, terminal modifications, or disulfide state.

The row-based charge/Gram-contrast Spearman correlations are −0.199 and −0.255. For equal-component weights, every row receives weight 1 / component size within Venomics, so each represented component receives the same total weight. Exact weighted midrank ECDFs are computed for both variables, followed by weighted Pearson correlation. Unit weights are checked against ordinary Spearman for each source/version. Weighted correlations are +0.260 and +0.270. A separate component-median analysis gives +0.253 and +0.273.

These are different estimands. Inverse weighting does not establish the true biological association, and component medians change both the weighting and the data representation. The sign reversal demonstrates aggregation sensitivity. The composition-adjusted rank-residual correlations remain negative, showing why that adjustment alone does not address representation by related variants. Sensitivity to dropping large components further documents their influence. The graph is the existing terminal-extension/one-substitution single-linkage construction, not a complete homology partition or a guarantee of independence.

Evidence: source concentration, association/weighting table, large-component sensitivity, spectrum/aggregation figure.

The figure below compares cross-version target-contrast preservation on the left and the Venomics charge-proxy relationship under alternative weighting on the right. Its two panels address preservation and sampling influence separately.

Sequence-level disagreement extension

The focused explanation is SEQUENCE_FINDINGS.md. sequence_disagreement.py reads existing predictions, source assignments, the broader sequence-component map, and the earlier exact- composition pairs. It performs no new model inference. The manifest records the raw/dependency hashes, software versions, definitions, and 15 passing checks. All reported effects remain exploratory properties of the saved prediction matrix.

Exact local edits

All equal-length one-substitution pairs with length at least eight are found using equal-position deletion signatures. All members of a signature bucket are paired, then source-mismatched pairs are excluded. This gives 41,253 pairs in 3,354 represented components. It differs from the earlier component graph's edge count because that graph used a sufficient set of linking edges rather than enumerating every pair in a multi-member signature bucket.

Every pair's sequence identity, length, and mutated position are checked directly; duplicate pairs are excluded, and both members must lie in the same precomputed component. Components are still single-linkage connected groups, not independent biological families. Most observed pairs come from the database and challenge collections; the pair distribution is not a random sample of possible mutations. Pairs and response fields are retained in a deterministic compressed CSV.

The main values are log2 MIC predictions, each model's within-cohort percentile, and three disagreement scores: raw log range, model-median-centered log range, and within-model percentile range. For models A and B and sequences s and t,

change in log prediction gap = [z_A(t) − z_B(t)] − [z_A(s) − z_B(s)].

The same change is independently checked as the difference between the two models' individual edit responses. An arbitrary constant intercept for either model cancels, which is also checked. Thus local differential responses can be examined without assuming that absolute model scales are experimentally calibrated. Range and percentile scores remain definition-dependent and are reported separately.

Local coherence reference

Let d(i) be a disagreement score and G(i) the other sequences from the same source and exact length. The reference for anchor i is the mean of abs(d(i) − d(j)) over j in G(i), excluding i. Each observed neighbor pair uses the average of its two anchor references. This conditions on the observed anchors rather than comparing the neighbor set to an unmatched global sample.

Expected distances are computed by sorting within groups and using cumulative sums, avoiding a quadratic distance matrix. The scalar and grouped formulas are checked against explicit distance matrices, including grouped ties. A second reference subtracts all contributions from the anchor's own component and excludes cells without a remaining comparator. No randomization p value is inferred.

For the rank score, equal-pair means are 0.1134 locally and 0.2113 for the source/ length reference; equal-component means are 0.0910 and 0.2145. The ratio is below one in all eight sources under both weightings. This shows local coherence of disagreement, but one-substitution neighbors also share composition and may share training exposure. The reference does not isolate a residue-order mechanism.

Evidence: local/reference results, locality and example figure.

The figure below places the ordinary local-neighbor/reference comparison beside one selected strong opposing edit. The example shows a possible exception, rather than the frequency of the ordinary response.

Large responses and examples

A strong opposite response requires both models to change by at least the specified absolute log2 margin and to change in opposite directions. At a one-log2 margin, the APEX/AMPredictor count is 298 of all 41,253 pairs, spread across 41 components. The 15.7% opposing fraction among its 1,902 eligible large-response pairs must not be confused with its 0.72% fraction of all pairs. Equal-component averaging further reduces the all-pair rate to 0.30%.

The other model-pair results and half-log2 margins are retained. These margins describe response size; they do not estimate assay error or identify experimental activity cliffs. A large change in disagreement can occur when models agree on the direction but differ in response magnitude.

The D4I example is a selected illustration, not a representative edit. Both sequences lack exact matches in the two cached exposure lists, but broader homology, other models' training sets, chemistry, and complete inference provenance remain unresolved. The K12L example in the same catalogue has an AMPredictor training-list match for one member; it is expressly not an independent validation case. Examples are restricted to cysteine-free sequences of length 8–39, with at most one selected example per existing component. Selecting examples after observing their responses cannot confirm a sequence rule.

Evidence: opposing-response counts, score changes, example values and exposure flags, all mutation-type summaries, source/component-subset summaries.

Rearrangement classes and order features

The 5,410 earlier two-member composition/source-matched pairs are classified using only the two sequences. For mutually exclusive summaries, a letter rotation is classified first, then an adjacent swap, a separated swap, and other reorderings. A letter rotation is a string operation, not chemical peptide cyclization. The exclusive adjacent category contains 284 pairs. Counting adjacent swaps regardless of the rotation category adds one overlapping pair, giving 285; the number of twofold responses remains 2, 53, and 24 for APEX, MBC, and AMPredictor.

Five arrangement features are retained: longest K/R run, longest run from the hydrophobic proxy set A/I/L/M/F/W/V/Y, adjacent K/R pairs, the K/R count in the first three minus last three positions, and a circular hydrophobic-run descriptor. The circular descriptor is checked to be invariant under letter rotations. It is a control for separating changed endpoints from rearranged internal order, not a model prediction or an assertion that the peptides are cyclic.

Comparisons are oriented toward the sequence with the greater feature value. They therefore estimate a within-composition descriptive association; several features can change together. Five feature summaries are reported for raw, centered, and rank scores. No claim is made that an exhaustive motif search was performed or that the selected feature has an independent causal effect.

For dependence sensitivity, components touching a composition pair are linked in a small additional graph, giving 2,187 pair components across the 5,410 pairs. Equal-pair-component averaging uses those groups, which may contain different old components joined through an anagram pair. They are not assumed independent. Two deterministic component subsets and source strata are additional sensitivity checks chosen after exploration, not held-out confirmation of a preregistered hypothesis. Cysteine-free length-8–39 and non-rotation restrictions are reported.

The longest hydrophobic-run association remains negative across these checks, but the mean effect is only about 0.02 rank-score units. Basic-run and terminal- position associations are less consistent in some subsets. Neither agreement nor a particular order feature has been validated against activity labels here.

Evidence: exclusive edit classes, all adjacent swaps, feature summaries, source/subset checks, disjoint component subsets, pair classification, arrangement figure.

The figure below contrasts twofold responses by observed rearrangement category with rank-gap changes associated with simple arrangement features. Category sizes and weighting differ, so bar heights are not experimental edit effects.

Cysteine, charge, and global profiles

The first-cysteine analysis reorients all observed single substitutions so that the cysteine-free member is the baseline and the other member introduces exactly one C. Other residue identity changes at the same time, so this is not an isolated effect of cysteine chemistry. The 1,667 pairs occupy 111 components; three supply 54.8% of the pairs. The mean rank-score change is −0.0359 per pair but +0.0219 under equal-component weighting, and centered-range signs also differ. This prevents a universal first-cysteine disagreement rule. It does not establish accuracy within or outside any model's training composition.

For a separate profile comparison, high/low tails are defined for each score and compared only within source/exact-length cells containing both groups. A cell's feature-mean difference receives weight equal to the smaller group mass. With unit row weights, the sum of those masses is the maximum possible matching capacity, not a particular randomly selected set of pairs. With inverse within- source component-size weights, the mass is fractional and must not be called a sample size. These comparisons do not condition on predicted potency.

The rank-tail comparison has 287 common cells and unweighted capacity 5,505. Some pooled charge and cysteine associations remain, but source-specific signs and the effect of weighting limit their interpretation. A between-sequence composition association and the response to a local replacement are different estimands and need not have the same sign. These results concern prediction disagreement, not evidence that any sequence is biologically unreliable.

Evidence: first-C summary, first-C source/subset checks, matched profiles, check results.

Similar MIC predictions with divergent rankings: focused subanalysis

Reading path: the agreement report now presents the subgroup and its limitations as a current narrative; its interpretation remains supporting rather than central. The curated core report emphasizes screening decisions; the main report uses the same seven section titles as its detailed companions. Exploratory target-panel and source-aggregation results have a current home in wider output patterns. Earlier duplicate report snapshots were removed after their substantive analyses were consolidated.

Question, cohort, and thresholds

similar_mic_different_ranks.py uses the same 194,947 unique complete-case sequences and the three E. coli export columns. All inputs remain unchanged. SHA-256 of the input TSV is ef8ced4ef2a260fced7e47b2d6b2ca415793e356a2d94997b1329ce464cac600.

For sequence i, define MIC spread = max_j log2(MIC_ij) − min_j log2(MIC_ij) and rank gap = max_j percentile_ij − min_j percentile_ij. Percentiles are average tied ranks divided by 194,947, calculated separately for each model on this identical set. Primary MIC agreement is spread ≤1 (largest/smallest MIC ≤2); primary divergent ranking is gap ≥0.50. These cutoffs are descriptive choices, not validated experimental error tolerances. They were not chosen by optimizing a sequence association.

Primary results: 1,478 MIC-agreed sequences, 1,155 meeting both criteria, 0.758% and 0.592% of the collection respectively. The conditional fraction is 78.146%. The median joint-group rank gap is 71.861 percentage points. Counts vary across MIC ratios 1.1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 4, 8, and 16, crossed with rank gaps 25, 50, and 75 points; all 21 combinations are exported. None is a confirmatory hypothesis test.

All three pairwise comparisons use the same complete-case denominator. At twofold, agreement is 9,252 for APEX/MBC, 4,669 for APEX/AMPredictor, and 80,156 for MBC/AMPredictor. The corresponding joint ≥50-point counts are 5,240, 3,468, and zero. In all 1,155 three-model primary cases, APEX has the most favorable percentile. This distinction should accompany general claims about “the models”: the joint phenomenon is not equally represented in all pairs.

Distribution explanation and example selection

The script looks up fixed MIC values in each model's original full-cohort distribution. At 32 µM the percentiles are 2.985%, 71.184%, and 81.069% for APEX, MBC, and AMPredictor. This directly explains how equal values can occupy different ranks. It is not an accuracy evaluation or a calibrated reference distribution. For observed values, lookup exactly reproduces average tied ranks; for unobserved reference values it uses the empirical fraction below that value.

Illustrative sequences are sorted by smallest MIC spread in the primary subgroup, keeping one per observed sequence component. The first is PLKRLLKLRLLL, with predictions 17.670568, 17.766088, and 17.453678 µM; percentiles 0.853%, 54.630%, and 67.006%. It is selected to illustrate the numerical point, not as an unbiased representative or a laboratory recommendation.

Sequence descriptors and comparisons

Every sequence contributes equal weight to the primary profile. K/R and D/E are counted literally; hydrophobic fraction is A/I/L/M/F/W/V/Y divided by length. Charge proxy is (K+R−D−E)/length, without histidine, termini, pH, or modifications. Residue composition, Shannon composition entropy, cysteine presence, absence of D/E, and positive charge-proxy frequency are exported. Pooled-residue composition is separately labeled because it weights longer peptides more.

The subgroup median length is 14 (IQR 12–17), mean K/R fraction 28.133%, mean D/E fraction 1.096%, mean hydrophobic fraction 54.313%; 97.056% lack C and 86.753% lack D/E. It spans 762 observed broader sequence components; the largest five account for 9.870%. Components are defined by the pre-existing terminal-extension and eligible one-substitution graph. Connected components are an imperfect dependence control, not curated families.

Two controls answer different questions: (a) all 193,792 sequences outside the primary subgroup; (b) the 323 sequences satisfying MIC agreement but falling below the rank-gap cutoff. Matching dimensions are source and exact length, optionally adding floor(median of the three log2 MICs / bin width). Bin widths are 1, 0.5 (primary), and 0.25. Because the three-member median is used, this is also log2 of the middle predicted MIC. Fixed bins have boundary effects; the sensitivity grid assesses some of that dependence.

Within each common bin, calculate a weighted mean for target and control. The overall contrast is the average within-bin difference, weighted by the smaller target/control mass in that bin. The first weighting gives every sequence weight 1. The second gives weight 1 / number of complete-case sequences in that source-component, reducing contributions from large related groups. It is not a bootstrap, propensity model, or effect estimate under a causal assignment mechanism. No p-values are reported for these selected exploratory contrasts.

Against the full remaining collection at primary bin width, differences in K/R, D/E, hydrophobic fraction, and cysteine-presence frequency are +0.953, −0.532, +2.227, and −6.848 percentage points. With source-component weighting they are +1.815, −0.508, +3.061, and −9.045 points. These directions persist under the implemented alternative bin widths, but magnitude is baseline-dependent. Exact-length matching necessarily produces zero length contrast; this is explicitly checked. Comparisons condition on predicted MIC and therefore cannot identify a causal sequence mechanism.

Support must be considered before interpreting control (b). The median middle MIC is 31.308 µM in the target group and 300.078 µM in control (b). At the primary matching width, 76 target sequences occur in common bins, and the sum of smaller unweighted bin counts is only 45 (3.896% of target n). These are overlap diagnostics, not actual paired samples or independent replicate counts. Different definitions of matching support are exported side by side. General claims about a distinctive motif separating the two kinds of MIC agreement are unsupported.

A limited order-specific check within this subgroup

The script also calculates adjacent K/R-pair and adjacent hydrophobic-pair counts, subtracting the expected count under random permutation of the same sequence composition. For n residues of a type in a sequence of length L, the expected number of adjacent same-type pairs is n(n−1)/L; the excess is divided by L−1. This expectation is checked against exhaustive permutations of a toy sequence. These residuals describe local clustering, not helicity, amphipathicity, or a complete motif search.

The target mean excess is −0.00952 for K/R pairs and −0.02424 for hydrophobic pairs. Relative to the source/length/MIC-matched full remaining collection, the differences are −0.01032 and −0.01339; with component weighting, −0.01330 and −0.01119. Thus, the composition profile does not imply extra clustering of these residue types. These small selected contrasts do not establish a positional mechanism or a unique motif. Structural predictions, sliding-window scans, and position-specific enrichment have not been performed here.

Population sensitivity and verification

Population MIC agreement / n Joint cases using original rank reference Joint fraction among MIC agreement
Full common set 1,478 / 194,947 1,155 78.15%
Cysteine-free, length 8–39 1,332 / 122,813 1,101 82.66%
Exclude exact cached APEX/AMPredictor corpus matches 1,356 / 191,921 1,057 77.95%
One deterministic representative per broader component 760 / 110,491 524 68.95%

Representatives use the smallest SHA-256 sequence hash within a component, so selection does not use predictions. These population checks preserve the original reference ranks; the export separately recomputes ranks in each restricted population (changing the question). The recomputed joint counts are 1,009, 1,062, and 523 in the three restricted populations. Restricting cached exact matches cannot prove independence from all training or homologous data. The representative sensitivity shows that the headline conditional rate is partly collection-dependent; it remains a majority in this restriction.

An additional independent recomputation from the raw TSV, using sorted-value rank lookups instead of pandas ranks, confirmed exported subgroup membership, counts, the example ratio, median length, cysteine absence (1,121/1,155), and D/E absence (1,002/1,155).

All 12 automated checks passed: denominator; finite positive log predictions and mapping coverage; direct ratios versus log differences; target subset inclusion; empirical tied ranks for each of three models; the adjacency expectation; source-count reconciliation; both disjoint-control definitions; and zero exact-length contrasts. These checks validate implementation identities, not experimental accuracy. The manifest records input hash, package versions, definitions, elapsed time, and scope.

Outputs: manifest, checks, all agreed sequences, threshold grid, profiles, matched contrasts, support, population sensitivity, and figure.

The figure below shows how common the defined concentration agreement is and illustrates why one nearly equal predicted concentration can occupy very different percentiles across models.

Screening rules, matched targets, and controlled sequence-order responses

Purpose and interpretive revision

The user questioned whether within-model relative placement was sufficiently informative and whether different outputs actually measured the same thing. The revised core reports reduce emphasis on the MIC-agreement/rank subgroup. A percentile is a function of a prediction and the model's full-cohort distribution; an equal MIC can occupy a different percentile without disagreement about that peptide's predicted concentration. The earlier frequencies remain correct under their definitions, but neither those frequencies nor their selected composition profile establish a new biological mechanism. The subgroup remains reproducible and is retained in the preliminary analyses.

The new screening_decision_trends.py investigates (1) fixed-concentration selection, (2) same-strain APEX and within-head DeepAMP decisions, (3) general AMP classifier decisions, and (4) composition-controlled DeepAMP order responses. This is exploratory analysis of the exported prediction table, not a model benchmark against independent measurements. No inference, calibration fitting, downloads, or input changes are performed.

Cohorts and matching outputs

The full TSV contains 195,625 unique sequence rows. The three E. coli regressors share 194,947 complete cases. Each DeepAMP paired comparison has 190,876 complete cases, and the four classifiers have 195,620. Length/cysteine-restricted cohorts are formed within each comparison, not forced to have the E. coli cohort's denominator: for example, DeepAMP's cysteine-free length-8–39 set has 122,823 sequences, versus 122,813 for the three-regressor set. Missing predictions are never treated as rejections.

Eight APEX version targets are matched by metadata strain indices, excluding alias-unverified outputs in either version. DeepAMP CNN and LSTM are paired separately within their Gram-negative and Gram-positive output groups. These are matched declared output categories, not identical assay-condition predictions. APEX versions are related models; DeepAMP architecture, training, fitted weights, and preprocessing are not a controlled ablation. The earlier DeepAMP replay establishes a small sampled reconstruction of exported predictions, not general accuracy.

The pre-existing broader component map covers the 194,947-sequence E. coli common cohort. It covers 190,198 of the 190,876 DeepAMP-paired sequences, so component-representative sensitivities omit 678 eligible but unmapped sequences. No fictional singleton components are assigned. Representatives minimize a SHA-256 hash of the sequence, independently of predictions. DeepAMP yields 108,657 representatives. Component definitions capture observed extensions/substitutions, not all homology. Coverage is explicitly exported.

Fixed-concentration selection and denominators

Cutoffs are 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, and 128 µM, with passage defined as prediction ≤ cutoff. They are illustrative operational choices, not experimentally justified breakpoints. Predictions are in declared exported µM; no new unit transformation is applied. A shared numeric cutoff does not make the E. coli endpoints biologically identical or compensate for different calibration/training-label conventions.

At 16 µM, APEX/MBC/AMPredictor pass 1,362/100,676/126,192 of 194,947 (0.699%/51.643%/64.731%). All three pass 897; at least one passes 144,361. Source-specific rates preserve the same ordering in all eight sources, and the implemented length/cysteine and component-representative populations preserve the broad contrast. These are not inferred active-peptide prevalences. Source collections have different histories and selection rules.

For each pair, four cells are exported: joint passage, left-only passage, right-only passage, joint rejection. Reporting only overall agreement can hide disagreement in the selected pool. APEX E. coli at 16 µM has 736 joint passages, 1,959 old-only, 626 new-only, and 192,304 joint rejections. Overall agreement is 98.679%, but 2,585 of the 3,321 sequences passing at least one version receive discordant decisions (77.838%). The low all-sequence discordance and high selected-pool discordance are both correct. Neither is an error rate against experiments.

A margin sensitivity counts discordance when one prediction is ≤T/m and the other >T*m, for m=1, √2, and 2. At m=1 this must reproduce ordinary cutoff discordance, which is checked. At T=16,m=2 the criteria are ≤8 versus >32 µM. For APEX/MBC, APEX/AMPredictor, and MBC/AMPredictor the counts are 61,597, 84,324, and 13,429. The margins describe numerical separation, not experimental uncertainty or a universally acceptable MIC error.

Target-matched decision differences

Here, pass means predicted MIC ≤16 µM and fail means >16 µM. Discordance means exactly one pass. The overall denominator is all 190,876 sequences with paired predictions; the selected-pool denominator includes only peptides passing at least one model. A strict twofold margin instead requires one prediction ≤8 µM and the other >32 µM. A head is the output trained for a particular target.

For DeepAMP at 16 µM, CNN/LSTM discordance is 41,165/190,876 (21.566%) for Gram-negative and 38,421/190,876 (20.129%) for Gram-positive. Within the union of passing sequences the corresponding fractions are 54.935% and 47.002%. Median per-peptide LSTM/CNN prediction ratios are 1.01362 and 0.94801. At the strict m=2 margin, counts are 11,646 and 11,685 (6.101%/6.122% of all paired eligible sequences; 28.291%/30.413% of ordinary discordances).

The cysteine-free length-8–39 restriction gives ordinary discordance 23.013%/21.067%; component representatives give 15.141%/14.650%. These sensitivities show collection dependence while retaining substantial differences. A near-unity median ratio does not characterize individual prediction agreement. The native Gram-head labels are retained for table lookup. The 9 November paper review identifies E. coli/B. subtilis training measurements for the two heads; broad pooled-species interpretations are not supported. Neither head provides an independently established exact assay match for arbitrary input sequences.

Classifier decisions and pipeline interaction

A positive vote means exported classifier score ≥0.5. Unanimity includes either all four positive or all four negative; mixed means one, two, or three positive. Each fraction below divides by sequences with all four scores unless stated otherwise. These labels describe activity classifications rather than a concentration estimate.

The four exports are MACREL, AI4AMP, AMP-CLIP, and AMPlify. At a common exploratory 0.5 score rule, individual positive fractions are 46.829%, 60.947%, 47.659%, and 61.838%. Four-way outcomes are 42,645 unanimously positive (21.800%), 24,878 unanimously negative (12.718%), and 128,097 mixed (65.482%). These use 195,620 classifier-complete rows; the old MIC-common unanimity count of 42,643 uses a different denominator.

Observed four-way unanimity is 34.517%, versus 12.559% under independent labels with the same global model-specific positive fractions. Under independent within-source/exact-length label assignments preserving those model-specific stratum rates, expected unanimity is 19.009%. The expectation is computed analytically as the row-weighted product of four positive probabilities plus the product of four negative probabilities. These hypothetical random-label references do not provide ground truth or significance; shared sequence features beyond length and source, training information, and other factors can contribute to excess agreement. They prevent interpreting the mixed-decision fraction alone as evidence that the tools are unrelated. All reference values are exported.

The 16 vote patterns and each model's only-positive/only-negative counts are exported. Pairwise agreement is 56.887–70.077%, with Cohen's kappa approximately 0.147–0.400. Positive agreement is 2*joint_positive/(left_positive+right_positive); negative agreement is the corresponding negative formula. Cohen's kappa uses chance agreement calculated from the two marginal positive fractions. It is not PABAK, not a correctness metric, and can be affected by prevalence.

At score rules 0.3 and 0.7, mixed-decision fractions are 63.770% and 70.389%. AMP-CLIP is exported as binary 0/1 and its rule is unchanged at these thresholds. This sensitivity therefore varies three classifiers' score cutoffs alongside a fixed fourth decision, not four calibrated operating points. At 0.5, mixed decisions remain 59.534% in the cysteine-free length-8–39 set and 64.723% among mapped component representatives. Different activity-label definitions and training data can contribute; these general classifiers do not predict the same numerical E. coli endpoint as the regressors.

The script also exports unanimous classifier outcomes within each MIC-cutoff selection. These bridge tables describe pipeline interactions. They do not validate regression errors, establish true inactive sequences, or prove the benefit of a consensus filter.

Two additional classifier score rules

The rule-sensitivity script defines positive as score ≥0.3 or ≥0.7, with negative below the chosen boundary, alongside the baseline 0.5. AMP-CLIP's binary values remain unchanged. All three rules use the same 195,620 sequences and 41,253 observed one-substitution pairs. The script recalculates source/exact-length mean contrasts and the source/length neighbor reference after each reassignment; it does not reuse baseline group probabilities for the alternatives. Category weights are the smaller group count, and the pair summary weights every observed pair equally. Matched support can change with the score rule.

The section 4 companion explains the findings alongside the plot. Counts, matching support, baseline-to-alternative group transitions, 22 checks, and input hashes are saved in rule-sensitivity outputs. These checks do not create independent pairs or calibrated score thresholds.

Controlled sequence-order comparison

An order response compares predictions for two peptides with identical amino-acid counts in different orders. A twofold response counts a larger/smaller prediction ratio ≥2, regardless of direction. The percentage uses the retained pair count for each full or restricted comparison.

The pair list comes from the earlier additional-trends analysis: exactly two observed sequences per same-source composition group. Of 5,410 pairs, 5,306 have all four DeepAMP outputs. Each pair has identical amino-acid counts; length, composition-based charge proxy, hydrophobic fraction, and composition entropy are consequently fixed. Every sequence occurs in only one of these pairs, although related components can span multiple pairs.

For a canonical lexicographic pair orientation, compute delta = log2(MIC_right / MIC_left) for each model. Order-response size is abs(delta), with twofold defined as ≥1 and fourfold as ≥2. CNN/LSTM twofold fractions are 30.739%/51.225% for Gram-negative and 27.045%/49.152% for Gram-positive. Median fold changes are 1.435/2.059 and 1.385/1.965, respectively.

The LSTM twofold fraction exceeds CNN in seven of eight sources for both targets. The exception, marlys (86 pairs), has 26.744%/20.930% for Gram-negative and 19.767%/18.605% for Gram-positive. This prevents a universal source- or architecture-level claim. Other sources include 2,279 Extinctomics pairs, so source composition could influence pooled magnitude; source-specific exports are retained.

A cysteine-free length-8–39 restriction keeps 4,296 pairs. Rates remain 30.261%/52.444% and 26.304%/49.092%. This is a conservative sequence sensitivity, not certification that these sequences lie in the DeepAMP training distribution.

For a stronger dependence sensitivity, sort pair identifiers by SHA-256 of sequence_left|sequence_right, then greedily retain a pair only if neither of its component IDs has appeared in a previously retained pair. If both sequences share a component, that component is counted once. This retains 2,197 pairs without component reuse across pairs. CNN/LSTM rates remain 33.091%/51.934% and 27.765%/48.157%. The greedy subset is deterministic and model-independent, but it is not a random sample, and graph components are not complete biological-family definitions.

Direction disagreement requires opposite signs of delta. Requiring each model to have abs(delta)>1 yields 937 Gram-negative and 843 Gram-positive pairs; 335 (35.752%) and 284 (33.689%) have opposite signs. The > criterion for eligibility is deliberately distinguished from the ≥ criterion in the response-rate table. The same pairs are reused across targets, so the two outcomes are correlated rather than independent biological replications. Large responses and opposing preferences demonstrate learned-function differences; laboratory composition-matched measurements are needed to decide whether either response is appropriate.

Exploratory sequence composition of discordant DeepAMP selections

At 16 µM, the script compares CNN-only versus LSTM-only passing sequences. It reports unadjusted profiles and source/exact-length-stratified differences. Stratum weights are the smaller of the two group counts; support and represented counts are exported. The matched CNN-only-minus-LSTM-only K/R differences are +1.986 percentage points for Gram-negative and +2.956 for Gram-positive, while other descriptors differ in direction or magnitude across targets. These are selected-output associations; they do not identify a mechanism, control chemistry, or establish a causal residue effect. They remain supplementary rather than a new headline motif claim.

Verification, outputs, and reproduction

All 126 implementation checks passed. They include declared units and cohort coverage, finite positive MICs, threshold-count monotonicity, complete vote partitions, equivalence of m=1 margin and ordinary discordance, binary AMP-CLIP values, classifier score bounds, exact-length matched differences, four-cell partitions, source equality, identical composition, and absence of sequence reuse in the controlled pair set. Repeated checks across thresholds are implementation safeguards, not 126 independent scientific validations.

An independent raw-data recomputation confirmed all primary cutoff counts/intersections, all ten matched-target decision tables at all six cutoffs, classifier consensus, controlled-pair composition/source/component annotations, absence of component reuse in the greedy subset, all four primary order-response tables by explicit sequence lookup, and the unchanged TSV hash. This is computational verification on the same data, not independent biological evidence.

Run python analysis_review/screening_decision_trends.py after the stress-test component map and additional-trends composition pairs have been generated. The script writes to outputs/screening_decision_trends. The manifest records the unchanged input hash, package versions, cohort counts, cutoffs, execution time, and scope. The original notebook and older numerical analyses need not be rerun for presentation changes.

Primary tables: MIC cutoff counts, pairwise cutoff partitions, source-specific counts, matched-target decisions, coverage, margin sensitivities, classifier decisions, pairwise classifier agreement, controlled order responses, direction agreement, and pair membership. The order-response figure shows the full and restricted pair comparisons. The decision figure summarizes cutoff, matched-target, and classifier patterns without interpreting them as experimental accuracy.

Shortlist overlap and UpSet figure

An UpSet plot gives each exact selection combination its own bar. Filled dots name the models selecting that combination, while pale dots name models excluding it. Pair-only bars exclude triple-shared peptides; inclusive pairwise overlaps add them back. Fixed-budget lists have equal sizes; cutoff-selected lists need not.

The section-1 extension repeats the same complete-case calculation at top 2% and top 5%, using 3,899 and 9,748 entries per model after rounding upward. Triple intersections are 22 and 233. Membership, exact intersections, and checks are retained in top-2% outputs and top-5% outputs. The section 1 report displays both plots and compares overlaps with consistent denominators.

Spearman correlations compare the same sequences' prediction ranks across each model pair, both in the full 194,947-row cohort and separately within each source. Average tied ranks are used; agreement with Pearson correlation of those ranks and with the previous global estimates is checked. The correlations describe ordering over each stated population, not activity accuracy or ordering restricted to the shortlisted tail. Correlations and denominators · extension manifest. The rank-agreement subsection shows every source alongside the pooled estimate.

The 9 November report asks the fixed-budget question before concentration-cutoff comparisons: which peptides would be tested if each tool could nominate the same number? plot_shortlist_upset.py independently rebuilds the three E. coli lists from the unchanged raw TSV. It sorts sequences lexicographically, takes exactly ceil(0.01 × 194947) = 1950 lowest predictions per model, and enumerates the seven nonempty membership patterns. No selection boundary is tied. Native outputs remain only approximately matched: APEX ATCC 11775 versus broader E. coli targets in MBC/AMPredictor.

The exclusive cells sum to 5,674 selected sequences. Multiplying each cell by its number of selecting models and summing gives 5,850 selections, exactly 3 × 1,950. For each individual model, its membership cells sum to 1,950. The inclusive pairwise intersections are 36+6=42, 27+6=33, and 101+6=107, reproducing previous results. The new plot therefore changes presentation and adds the previously unreported full intersection breakdown; it does not change the shortlist definition. This is the selected three-tool comparison, not an exhaustive intersection of all MIC outputs. The model review also identifies an E. coli training basis for the DeepAMP negative head; its exclusion from this predefined triad should not be justified by claiming that it has no species-level E. coli basis.

The UpSet figure uses a linear count axis, count labels on every bar, and a dot matrix marking selecting models. Zero/absent models are shown with pale dots. Exclusive bars must not be read as inclusive pairwise counts. Only selected peptides are in the union table; nonselected sequences are not another plotted intersection.

Eight checks cover the cohort, list sizes, partition of the union, reconstruction of total and per-model selections, prior pairwise counts, independent set algebra, and untied boundaries. All passed. Outputs are PNG, PDF, SVG, exclusive counts, inclusive pairwise counts, all selected sequence memberships, and manifest. The same script creates separate concentration-cutoff, within-head decision, and classifier-vote panels from the already verified decision tables.
