Exact overlap at the 16 µM cutoff

The same plotting script now supports python analysis_review/plot_shortlist_upset.py --cutoff-only. It reads the unchanged primary three-model cohort and selects predictions ≤16 µM, then counts all eight membership combinations, including joint failures. The seven displayed passing combinations partition 144,361 peptides; 50,586 pass none. The individual totals are 1,362, 100,676, and 126,192, and the triple intersection is 897.

Seven checks verify cohort eligibility, the full and passing partitions, reconstructed model totals, agreement with prior cutoff totals, and independent set operations for every exact cell. Counts, all-sequence memberships, and manifest preserve the calculation. The plot and its interpretation appear together in the cutoff companion.

The cutoff UpSet below makes the exact membership breakdown visible. Its seven bars count peptides passing at least one tool; joint failures are reported separately above the plot.

Model review prompted by the comparison question

The updated MIC comparability audit links each model's paper and pinned adapter. It distinguishes matched labels from matched biological assays, and paper descriptions from checkpoint-specific training provenance. The most consequential correction is DeepAMP: the paper's negative and positive models use E. coli and B. subtilis MIC measurements respectively, rather than establishing pooled activity across whole Gram classes. It also mixes MIC training with artificial log-MIC = 4 labels for non-AMP examples. Previous broad-Gram wording in the report was too strong. Export column names are preserved; plot titles now annotate the paper-reported species.

MBC-Attention's species-level target averages repeated measurements across conditions; it is not the same target as a strain-specific APEX head. AMPredictor's reported training composition excludes cysteine and lengths ≥40, even if adapters accept longer inputs. APEX 1.1 codes inactive labels at 512 µM. These differences do not invalidate a comparison of the tools' selections, but they prevent attributing every difference to model error, isolated architecture, or a biological residue mechanism. General AMP classifier agreement does not validate a quantitative MIC, and the 16 µM screening rule is not claimed to reproduce the models' native binary classifications.

The adapter review also confirms that MBC removes its configured scale/bias before inverse-log conversion, and that the exported concentration values should not be exponentiated a second time. Code review and the existing sampled DeepAMP replay do not constitute a complete reconstruction of all model exports. Metadata and the original table remain unchanged; a separate review record stores annotations and evidence URLs.

A sensitivity prompted by artificial inactive labels asks whether the order-response contrast also exists where both sequences' CNN/LSTM predictions are ≤128 µM within a head. It retains 2,963 pairs for the E. coli-trained head and 3,331 for B. subtilis. Twofold response rates are CNN/LSTM 17.95%/46.98% and 15.55%/45.21%. Thus the direction also occurs outside the high-prediction tail, but conditioning on model outputs cannot isolate a causal pseudo-label effect or supply validation. review_mic_model_scope.py writes these and the 32 µM/10^3.5 sensitivities to the supporting table.

Venomics source comparison

  • The Venomics script uses the same 194,947-sequence primary MIC cohort, including all 4,618 Venomics sequences. It compares that source with the other 190,329 sequences and with each source separately. Source-level classifiers are evaluated on this shared set, rather than mixing them with the larger classifier-only cohort.

  • Feature averages first give each sequence equal weight. A second view uses inverse component size within each source, giving every represented source-group equal influence. The graph is the existing observed terminal-extension/one-substitution map. Its components are not independent evolutionary families, and a component can span sources.

  • The matched comparison uses exact length and cysteine presence, then adds K/R bins ten percentage points wide. Within each shared category, other-source rates are averaged using Venomics' category mass. This standardizes the comparator to the Venomics population; it differs from the minimum-group weighting used for the section 4 classifier contrasts. Unweighted and inverse-group-weighted versions are both exported. Five- and twenty-point K/R bins and one-source-at-a-time comparisons check dependence on those choices. Coverage is reported as retained Venomics sequence count or group-weight mass, according to the weighting.

  • Within-source shortlists take ceil(fraction × source count), with fractions 1%, 2%, 5%, and 10%. The 5% Venomics lists contain 231 entries. Exact membership cells include joint failures in the audit table, although the UpSet displays only the seven passing combinations. Group-median and twenty prediction-independent representative selections repeat the ranking comparison on 401 group entries, with 21 nominations each.

  • The source paper and the repository's import code establish prediction-based selection history. The eleven-target APEX 1.0 median check is a diagnostic of that history, not a reconstruction of every original filtering step or a laboratory test. Its multi-target 32 µM rule differs from the current single-target APEX 1.1 16 µM rule.

  • The section 6 companion embeds all four figures alongside definitions, denominators, and limitations. The manifest records inputs and the primary checks; the separate verification script uses raw sequence counts, NumPy sorting, explicit matched-cell loops, and earlier source correlations to check the reported arithmetic. New files are isolated in outputs/venomics, preserving earlier numerical results.

Source-stratified comparisons across the main dimensions

  • The source analysis extends the source-specific questions beyond Venomics. The source comparison report explains ranking, concentration decisions, matched-target decisions, classifier composition and neighbor agreement, and order-response findings with their own source counts.

  • Within-source shortlists use ceil(fraction × eligible count), comparing 1%, 2%, 5%, and 10% on the 194,947-sequence primary MIC set. The 5% checks also use group-median predictions, twenty deterministic hash-selected representatives per source-group, and C-free length-8–39 restrictions. Group summaries change the eligible units, rather than estimate corrected peptide rankings. Representatives share the same group count but can choose different sequence variants. Their ranges are not uncertainty intervals.

  • Matched-target tables separately use all paired DeepAMP outputs (190,876 sequences) or E. coli APEX versions (195,625). Counts of both-pass, both-fail, and exactly-one-pass decisions are computed at 8, 16, and 32 µM. A further check counts only disagreements where the predictions lie well to either side of the cutoff. Overall disagreement divides exactly-one-pass counts by every eligible pair of predictions; selected-pool disagreement divides by peptides passing either model. Group weights exclude unmapped entries and record that subset's size. All source rates are descriptive, not error estimates.

  • The classifier sequence comparison uses the primary set. Within each collection, it compares positive and negative groups at the same length, then averages those differences. Each length receives weight based on how much of the smaller group is available, before or after reducing large related groups' influence. Observed one-residue neighbors reuse the existing 41,253-pair catalogue; the reference now considers peptides in the primary MIC set rather than the larger classifier-only set. Observed same-group fractions are unchanged; reference probabilities can differ slightly. Pair-group reweighting is also exported.

  • Order responses are recomputed from raw DeepAMP concentrations for every source and target, using the 5,306 original composition-matched pairs, the 2,197-pair no-group-reuse subset, and target-specific subsets with all four predictions ≤128 µM. Source-balanced summaries average the eight fractions equally rather than pool the pairs. This changes sampling influence without creating independent experiments or identifying a correct biological average.

  • Ten primary checks reproduce prior shortlist intersections and matched-target decisions and reconcile source/pair partitions. A separate verifier passes 226 arithmetic checks using raw-array nomination sets, independently chosen representatives, explicit length-category contrasts, and concentration-ratio response tests. Definitions and hashes, verification results, and all new tables preserve the extension. Existing inputs, notebooks, and previous numerical results remain unchanged.

Analysis map

The detailed report follows one argument: prediction tools change screening choices, and sequence controls help describe how. Each final section now has one detailed companion, indexed in the README. Other preliminary analyses collects branches outside that argument, and reproducibility holds implementation results. This map gives each substantive analysis a current reading destination, including results that weakened an earlier interpretation. Earlier numerical calculations are preserved; current consolidated reports provide their reviewed interpretation.

Follow the question that matters

If the concern is whether the shortlist differences survive reasonable challenges, read the robustness report. If it is why a peptide can look “agreed upon” under one rule and disputed under another, read the agreement report. For shared target structure and collection effects, read the wider output report. For the recovered laboratory panel and the obstacles to an accuracy claim, read experimental-data recovery.

The established focused reports cover sequence changes, MIC variability, model differences, and validation. Supplementary here means a supporting result, sensitivity check, or provisional diagnostic; it does not mean every finding has equivalent evidential strength.

The reviewed notebook, section by section

Section numbers refer to damp_secondary_analysis.ipynb. The table separates the question from its role in the report, so a result does not disappear merely because it is unsuitable as a headline.

Notebook section Question and current destination Why it has that role
1. Reproducibility and semantics Validation, coverage and native outputs, model conversions Establishes calculation and output meaning, rather than biological correctness.
2. Provenance, composition, coverage Source composition and missingness Defines which collection and eligible sequences each result describes.
3. APEX version drift Main matched-target result, label-scale check Same strain is useful; changed labels and training prevent a simple causal interpretation.
4. Approximate E. coli agreement Main shortlist and cutoff results, budget and reference checks Supports practical selection differences, with only approximate endpoint matching.
5. DeepAMP outputs and extremes DeepAMP output patterns Head meanings and artificial inactive labels qualify extreme-value interpretations.
6. Classification disagreement Classifier-group sequence analysis, pairwise metrics and native AMP-Read Classifier votes are separate from quantitative MIC estimates; sequence profiles and neighbor transitions describe their structure.
7. Sequence associations Definition-dependent profiles, Venomics weighting Pooled residue/length associations do not establish a general mechanism.
8. APEX target spectrum Matched-panel decomposition Full panels are unequal; a direct version comparison needs the same targets.
9. Shortlist stability and limits Main cutoff result, robustness Selection counts are operational results, not true active fractions.
10. Target-coverage follow-up Matched spectrum and residuals Corrects the initial impression created by comparing 34 with 11 targets.
11. Budget and source composition Budget, source quotas, and population checks Tests whether the headline depends on one budget or collection.
12. Length-stratified source effects Source and weighting effects, source/length sensitivity table Describes conditional source differences; source is not a randomized treatment.
13. Sanity checks Reproduction evidence, stress tests Arithmetic checks support implementation, not independent replication.
14. Extreme-tail sequence neighbors Related-sequence audit Motivated dependence checks; the selected 200-row tail is not a representative experiment.
15. MIC comparability Model review Corrects earlier DeepAMP target wording and checks unit adapters.
16. Low disagreement and domain restriction Agreement definitions, domain checks A low prediction spread is not validated confidence or an established training domain.
17. Pinned-weight replay Validation, padding sensitivity A sampled inference route reproduces; other routes and all-model reconstruction remain open.
18. Experimental error and correction Original diagnostic limits A tiny exposed sample cannot validate a confidence score or a general calibration.
19. Training overlap Original panel exposure, discordant-family neighbors Exact exposure and nearby training sequences qualify an apparent accuracy result.
20. Symmetric disagreement tails Tail profiles, matching support, and controls Definitions and weighting change apparent sequence rules.
21. MIC variability MIC-context report Condition differences are relevant but do not supply a universal error allowance.
22. Fixed-budget overlap Main UpSet result Exact membership is a direct screening result.
23. Cutoff and consensus decisions Main sections 2–4, classifier detail Makes denominators and pipeline rules explicit.
24. Controlled sequence order Main sequence result, sequence detail Composition controls support fitted-function differences; biological validation is missing.

The early EDA also preserves APEX per-sequence SD and CV, an individual extreme profile, ten largest spreads, collapsed-family comparisons, row disagreement scores, and pairwise statistics. These remain inspection tools. Family averages mix targets and versions, AMP-Read units remain unresolved, and selected extremes are not typical peptides. The wider output report explains why these should not be promoted into accuracy or assay-uncertainty claims.
